questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly two firms sell an identical product, simultaneously choose prices $p_1,p_2\ge0$, both have constant marginal cost $c>0$, and face market demand $D(p)$; the cheaper firm sells to the whole market and equal prices split demand equally. Which feature of the model makes a firm that is slightly cheaper than its rival capture the entire market demand?
options: Both firms have the same constant marginal cost $c$.
The firms choose prices simultaneously, not one after the other.
The products are identical, so only the price matters.
Demand $D(p)$ is continuous and nonincreasing in the price.

questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly two firms sell an identical product, simultaneously choose prices $p_1,p_2\ge0$, both have constant marginal cost $c>0$, and face market demand $D(p)$; the cheaper firm sells to the whole market and equal prices split demand equally. How does the equilibrium price compare with the price in a market of many price-taking firms that have the same marginal cost $c$?
options: It is higher, because two firms keep some market power.
It is lower, because the two firms undercut each other below $c$.
It is halfway between $c$ and the price a monopolist would set.
It is the same: both equal the marginal cost $c$.

questions.question: With demand $D(p)=100-p$ and constant marginal cost $c=10$ for both of two firms selling an identical product, the Bertrand equilibrium (firms simultaneously choose prices) has price $10$, while a duopoly with the same demand and cost in which the firms simultaneously choose quantities has equilibrium price $40$. Which feature of the Bertrand model explains its lower price?
options: The firms move one after the other, so the second firm undercuts the first.
The firms choose prices, so a small price cut wins the entire market demand.
The firms are price takers who set price equal to marginal cost by assumption.
The firms split the market equally at every price profile, which halves margins.

questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products, demand $D(p)=120-p$ and constant marginal cost $c=20$ for both firms, the cheaper firm sells to the whole market and equal prices split demand. Both firms charge $p_1=p_2=50$. What is firm 1's profit?

Two Bertrand duopolists sell identical goods at unit cost $20$; market demand is $D(p)=120-p$ and all consumers buy from the cheaper firm. Firm 1 sets $p_1=45$ while firm 2 sets $p_2=50$. How much profit does firm 1 make?

In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products, demand $D(p)=120-p$, marginal cost $c=20$, the cheaper firm takes the whole market and equal prices split it. At $p_1=p_2=50$ each firm earns $1050$. Is $(50,50)$ a Nash equilibrium?
options: Yes: both firms earn the same profit of $1050$.
Yes: charging $51$ instead would give firm 1 zero.
No: firm 1 earns more by charging $51$ instead.
No: firm 1 earns $29\cdot71=2059$ by charging $49$.

questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products, demand $D(p)=100-p$ and marginal cost $c=10$, the cheaper firm takes the whole market. Prices are $p_1=8$ and $p_2=15$. Which unilateral deviation shows that this profile is not a Nash equilibrium?
options: Firm 1 raises its price to $16$ and earns $0$.
Firm 2 lowers its price to $8$ to share the market.
Firm 1 lowers its price to $6$ to sell more units.
Firm 2 raises its price to $20$ to earn a higher margin.

questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly two firms sell an identical product, simultaneously choose prices $p_1,p_2\ge0$, both have constant marginal cost $c>0$, and face market demand $D(p)$; the cheaper firm sells to the whole market and equal prices split demand equally. The unique Nash equilibrium is $p_1=p_2=c$. Is it a strict Nash equilibrium, in which every deviation gives a strictly lower payoff?
options: Yes: a unique Nash equilibrium is automatically a strict one.
No: against $p_j=c$, any price above $c$ also earns zero.
Yes: every deviation to a price below $c$ gives a strict loss.
No: a firm earns a positive profit by raising its price above $c$.

questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products, demand $D(p)=100-p$ and marginal cost $c=10$, prices must be whole numbers, the cheaper firm takes the market and equal prices split it. Which profile, besides $(10,10)$, is a Nash equilibrium?

In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products, demand $D(p)=100-p$ and marginal cost $c=10$, the cheaper firm takes the market and equal prices split it; prices are continuous. Firm 2 charges $p_2=70$. What is firm 1's best response?
options: A price just below $70$

questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products, demand $D(p)=100-p$ and marginal cost $c=10$, the cheaper firm takes the market and equal prices split it. Firm 2 charges $p_2=30$. For which prices $p_1$ does firm 1 earn a strictly positive payoff?

In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products and marginal cost $c$, prices on a grid of step $h>0$ containing $c$ make $(c+h,c+h)$ a Nash equilibrium when $D(c+h)>0$. Why does the same profile fail to be an equilibrium when prices are continuous?
options: With continuous prices demand at $c+h$ is zero, so both firms already earn nothing there.
With continuous prices the tie rule gives the whole market to one firm at equal prices.
A firm can then undercut to a price strictly between $c$ and $c+h$.
With continuous prices a firm can raise its price slightly above $c+h$ and earn more.

questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly two firms sell an identical product, simultaneously choose prices $p_1,p_2\ge0$, both have constant marginal cost $c>0$, and face market demand $D(p)$; the cheaper firm sells to the whole market and equal prices split demand equally. The model assumes $D(c)>0$. Suppose instead $D(p)=0$ for every $p\ge c$, while $D(p)>0$ for $p<c$. What happens to the set of Nash equilibria?
options: No equilibrium exists, because neither firm can make a profit.
Every profile with both prices at least $c$ becomes an equilibrium.
The unique equilibrium moves to both prices strictly below $c$.
$(c,c)$ remains the unique equilibrium, with zero profits.

questions.question: Two Bertrand duopolists sell an identical product at common unit cost $c>0$; demand $D(p)$ is continuous and nonincreasing with $D(c)>0$, the cheaper firm serves the whole market and equal prices split it. Firm 1 prices at cost, $p_1=c$, while firm 2 charges $p_2>c$, so firm 1 sells to everyone at zero profit. Which change of price by a single firm raises that firm's payoff?
options: Firm 2 lowers its price to $c$ so that it shares the market with firm 1.
Firm 1 lowers its price below $c$ so that it sells a larger quantity.
Firm 1 raises its price slightly above $c$, staying below $p_2$.
Firm 1 raises its price above $p_2$, which ends its zero-margin sales.

questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products and continuous prices, both firms have marginal cost $c$, demand is $D(p)=\max\{(a-p)/b,0\}$ with $a>c>0$ and $b>0$, the cheaper firm takes the market and equal prices split it. Let $p^m=(a+c)/2$ be the monopoly price and $c<p_2\le p^m$. What is firm 1's set of best responses to $p_2$?
options: It is the single price just below $p_2$, say $p_2$ minus one cent.
It is $\{p_2\}$, since matching the rival guarantees half the market.
It is empty: every price below $p_2$ is beaten by one closer to $p_2$.
It is $\{c\}$, since pricing at cost always wins the whole market.

questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly two firms sell an identical product, simultaneously choose prices $p_1,p_2\ge0$, both have constant marginal cost $c>0$, and face continuous nonincreasing market demand $D(p)$ with $D(c)>0$; the cheaper firm sells to the whole market and equal prices split demand equally. Consider a profile with $c<p_1<p_2$. Which unilateral deviation shows that it is not a Nash equilibrium?
options: Firm 1 lowers its price to $c$ to secure the whole market for certain.
Firm 2 raises its price further, which does not change its zero profit.
Firm 2 charges a price slightly above $c$ and below $p_1$, earning a positive profit.
No deviation is profitable, because firm 1 already serves the whole market.

questions.question: In a Bertrand duopoly with identical products, demand $D(p)=\max\{80-p,0\}$ and marginal cost $c=10$, the cheaper firm takes the market and equal prices split it. Both firms charge $90$ and earn $0$. Is $(90,90)$ a Nash equilibrium?
options: No: firm 1 can charge $50$ and earn $40\cdot30=1200$.
Yes: undercutting to $89$ still sells nothing, so no small cut pays.
Yes: both firms earn the same profit, so neither envies the other.
No: firm 1 can charge $89.99$ and capture the whole market's profit.
